productivity.method: TFP is computed by growth accounting (Törnqvist index) from a Cobb-Douglas production function. Annual TFP growth is Δlog A = Δlog Y − (1 − s̄) Δlog K − s̄ Δlog L, where s̄ is the average of the labor share in the two adjacent years, and the TFP index is the cumulated growth rates rebased to 2000 = 100. The labor share is compensation of employees divided by compensation of employees plus consumption of fixed capital plus net operating surplus for Mainland Norway (SSB 09170, current prices). It is shown as a separate series. Its mean over the sample is 59.8 percent. Y is gross value added in Mainland Norway at constant 2023 prices (SSB 09189), L is total hours worked in Mainland Norway (SSB 09174), K is the net stock of fixed capital in Mainland Norway at constant 2023 prices (SSB 09181). Labor productivity is Y/L. No adjustment is made for capacity utilization, labor quality or self-employed income (which is part of the operating surplus).

The level of a principal component is a normalization. Here it is set so that the component's average equals the average of the manufacturing labor share over the past 30 years, the dashed line in the chart. The papercenters it on the mean of the manufacturing share over the component's own years, which moves the whole line by a constant only.

labor_shares.method: Labor shares are computed from the national accounts in current prices. Gross labor share = compensation of employees / (compensation of employees + consumption of fixed capital + net operating surplus). Net labor share = compensation of employees / (compensation of employees + net operating surplus). Taxes and subsidies on production are excluded from the denominator, and income of the self-employed is part of the operating surplus. For general government the operating surplus is essentially zero, so the mainland and total-economy shares are pulled up by the public sector. The series excluding general government (Mainland Norway minus general government, own aggregation) avoids this. The definitions follow Holm and Jasinski, «Lønnsandelen i industrien», Samfunnsøkonomen. The common component for manufacturing is the first principal component of the sectoral labor shares from the same paper, computed in real time. In the latest estimation window it explains 34.5 percent of the variance of the gross shares and 29.8 percent of the net shares.

nordic_productivity.method: Every series in this tile is my own calculation from national accounts data, with the same method for every country as in the productivity tile for Mainland Norway. Labor productivity is gross value added at constant prices divided by total hours worked. TFP is computed by growth accounting (Törnqvist index) from a Cobb-Douglas production function. Annual TFP growth is Δlog A = Δlog Y − (1 − s̄) Δlog K − s̄ Δlog L, where s̄ is the average of the labor share in the two adjacent years, and the index is the cumulated growth rates set to 100 in 2000. Y is gross value added at constant prices, L is total hours worked and K is the net stock of fixed assets at constant prices. The labor share is compensation of employees divided by compensation of employees plus gross operating surplus and mixed income. For Mainland Norway and for Norway's total economy the data are Statistics Norway's national accounts. For the other countries they are the national accounts as published by Eurostat, for the whole economy. TFP ends where the capital stock ends, which is earlier than the other series for some countries. Eurostat has no capital stock at constant prices for Iceland, so TFP is missing there. No adjustment is made for capacity utilization, labor quality or the labor income of the self-employed (which is part of mixed income).

europe_productivity.method: Every series in this tile is my own calculation from national accounts data, with the same method for every country as in the productivity tile for Mainland Norway. Labor productivity is gross value added at constant prices divided by total hours worked. TFP is computed by growth accounting (Törnqvist index) from a Cobb-Douglas production function. Annual TFP growth is Δlog A = Δlog Y − (1 − s̄) Δlog K − s̄ Δlog L, where s̄ is the average of the labor share in the two adjacent years, and the index is the cumulated growth rates set to 100 in 2000. Y is gross value added at constant prices, L is total hours worked and K is the net stock of fixed assets at constant prices. The labor share is compensation of employees divided by compensation of employees plus gross operating surplus and mixed income. For Mainland Norway and for Norway's total economy the data are Statistics Norway's national accounts. For the other countries they are the national accounts as published by Eurostat, for the whole economy. TFP ends where the capital stock ends, which is earlier than the other series for some countries. For the United States, Y is real GDP because its accounts have no long series for total value added at basic prices, K is the Bureau of Economic Analysis' quantity index for the net stock of private and government fixed assets, L is total hours worked as published by the OECD, and the labor share uses the income components the United States reports to the OECD. No adjustment is made for capacity utilization, labor quality or the labor income of the self-employed (which is part of mixed income).
